title: In 177 OpenNeuro subjects, the putamen leads the cortex by 0.7-1.5 s more in rare whole-brain BOLD dips, which mostly follow deep breaths, than in rare whole-brain BOLD rises
abstract: In rare, large drops of the whole-brain fMRI signal, most of which follow a deep breath, the putamen (a deep grey-matter nucleus) reaches its trough 0.7-1.5 s earlier, relative to the cerebral cortex, than it reaches its peak in rare, large rises of the same signal. This shows that the regional timing of brain-wide BOLD events is not one fixed lag map: in the striatum it depends on the kind of event. We searched ReadyNeuro, minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro fMRI at 1 s per frame with one subject per study, for frames where the cortical global signal (GS, the mean of all cortical parcels, standardised per run) was at least 3 standard deviations from its mean; event peaks are 0.25-0.28 % of frames. We fixed the study split before reading data, found the pattern in 86 discovery studies, pre-registered the tests, and repeated them in 91 other studies (73.7 h, 208 task labels). Narrow events (at most 3 s wide) came with frame-to-frame jumps and slice-wise changes, the signs of head motion. Wide negative events (3.9 per hour) were longer than wide positive events (2.1 per hour; median width 8 vs 5 s), followed an edge-of-brain motion signal 6-16 s earlier, and followed a recorded deep breath in 56 % of cases in an 8-study physiological pool (positive events 17 %, random times 16 %). In confirmation the pre-registered median putamen-minus-GS peak lag was -1.56 s in negative events (n = 282) and -0.10 s in positive events (n = 142); 37 of 46 studies with both kinds showed the difference (Wilcoxon p = 1.4e-5). Other estimates of the difference: 1.19 s (mixed model within studies, 95 % CI 0.81-1.57), 1.08 s after adjustment for event width and shape, 0.66 s by cross-correlation, and 0.65 s for events of the same width in the same study (p = 0.014). The difference is a property of wider events; events 4-5 s wide show little or none. After recorded deep breaths the putamen also led (median 0.77-1.33 s), but not significantly when grouped by subject. Limits: no slice-timing correction, so only the sign difference within runs is free of acquisition effects; sign and width are confounded; physiological pools are small; the cause of the positive events is unknown, and the lag does not classify single events better than width.

display.caption: Putamen timing in rare wide global BOLD events. A: mean sign-adjusted signal of cortex (solid) and putamen (dashed), each scaled to its peak, for negative (blue) and positive (orange) events in the confirmation set; the putamen leads only in negative events. B: putamen peak time minus cortical GS peak time per event, discovery and confirmation. C: study means for studies with both signs.

Two families of extreme global-signal frames (confirmation set). A: event width vs maximum DVARS; narrow events come with frame-to-frame jumps (motion or slice artefacts). B: mean event time course by family and sign. C: edge-shell DVARS; negative wide events follow a bump 6-16 s earlier (grey band, breath-related apparent motion).

Physiology in the confirmation pool (8 studies). A: respiratory variation around wide negative and positive events and random times; deep breaths come about 11 s before negative events. B: finger-pulse amplitude. C: cortical GS and putamen after recorded deep breaths (positive control); the putamen trough comes first.
